concepts.def: Hierarchical division of society into ranked groups based on power, wealth and status.
Davis and Moore (1945): inequality is necessary to motivate the most talented into the most important roles.
Society polarised into bourgeoisie (own means of production) and proletariat (sell labour); class conflict drives history.
Stratification involves class (economic), status (prestige) and party (power); more nuanced than Marx.
Weber's term for opportunities to gain valued resources (health, education, income) shaped by social position.
Measure of income inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all); UK around 0.36 (ONS).

walkthroughs.body_html:
Social Stratification — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Social Stratification brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Social Stratification.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Davis and Moore's functionalist theory argues inequality is:
options: Unnecessary
Necessary to motivate talent
A capitalist conspiracy
Disappearing

mcqs.q: Weber's three dimensions of stratification are class, status and:
options: Gender
Race
Party
Religion

mcqs.q: How did Marx define social class?
options: Marx defined class by occupational status like the Registrar General.
Wealthy elites secretly control society.
Marx defined class by how much money people earn.
By relationship to the means of production: the bourgeoisie own productive resources; the proletariat sell their labour. Class is a structural relationship, not just income level.
Wealthy elites secretly control society.
Marx defined class by occupational status like the Registrar General.
All working-class people are an underclass.
A distinct group develops a culture of welfare dependency and anti-social behaviour.
